Comparison of micro-aerobic and anaerobic
fermentative hydrogen production from corn straw
Dong Li a, Chenxi Jiao b, Wei He c, Zhiying Yan a, Yuexiang Yuan a,
Zhidong Li a, Yani Guo b, Xiaofeng Liu a,*
a Key Laboratory of Environmental and Applied Microbiology, Environmental Microbiology Key Laboratory of

a b s t r a c t
Micro-aerobic and anaerobic fermentative hydrogen productions were carried out in bottle
tests (150 mL) and scale-up bioreactors (10 L) using corn straw as a substrate. Hydrogen
yield of 41.6 mL/g (volatile solid, VS) obtained from scale-up experiment with optimal
oxygen addition of 0.28 mL/(g (total solid, TS)$day) was higher than that of 28.9 mL/g VS
without additional oxygen. Oxidation reduction potential was300~150 mV for micro-
aerobic fermentation, where it was560~360 mV for anaerobic fermentation. The
micro-aerobic condition had strong buffering ability and could tolerate a greater accu-
mulation of volatile fatty acid. Both micro-aerobic and anaerobic hydrogen production
were butyric acid-type fermentation. Microbial community analysis indicated the presence
of Citrobacter sp. and Escherichia sp., which were unique to micro-aerobic system, as well as
classical Enterococcus, Bacteroides, Peptoclostridium, Clostridium genera that existed in both
micro-aerobic and anaerobic fermentation.

Introduction
Anaerobic fermentative hydrogen production has been suc-
cessfully used to treat easily degradable carbohydrates such
as glucose, xylose, sucrose, lactose, molasses, and starch,
reviewed by Davila-Vazquez et al. [1]. Agricultural straw pro-
vides abundant raw material for biological hydrogen produc-
tion, and is mainly composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and
lignin, which are closely intertwined [2]. To date, studies of
biological hydrogen production from straw have focused on
pretreatment
approaches,
including
steam-explosion
[3],
ozone [4], white-rot fungal [5], calcium hydroxide [6], hydro-
chloric acid [7], and sulfuric acid [8] treatments, all of which
signiﬁcantly increased the hydrogen yield of straw.
Reith et al. [9] provided an extensive list of heterotrophic
bacteria that have been reported to produce hydrogen,
including strict anaerobes such as Clostridia, facultative an-
aerobes such as Enterobacter and Escherichia, and aerobes such
as Alcaligenes and Bacillus. In general, the aerobic metabolic
rate is higher than the anaerobic metabolic rate, and growth
rates of bacterial growth rates are higher under aerobic con-
ditions than under strictly anaerobic conditions. This is

because highly proliferative bacteria tend to produce more
extracellular hydrolytic enzymes, such as cellulase and
hemicellulase. According to the enzyme adsorption dynamics
model proposed by South et al. [10], this increased enzyme
concentration can improve the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic
material. Therefore, appropriate oxygen addition can theo-
retically promote straw hydrolysis and further enhance
hydrogen production when a mixed culture containing strict
anaerobes, facultative anaerobes, and aerobes is used as the
inoculum. Moreover, excess oxygen should inhibit strict an-
aerobes to produce hydrogen. However, this hypothesis has
not yet been tested. In this study, the feasibility of micro-
aerobic fermentative hydrogen production from corn straw
(CS) was evaluated by a bottle test. Furthermore, the effect of
oxygen addition on fermentative hydrogen production from
straw was investigated using a bench-scale experiment.
Materials and methods
Substrates and inoculum
For the CS, air-dried CS was obtained from rural Chengdu,
China. The collected CS was chopped and ground into small
particles that were less than 1 mm in size for use as substrate.
The total solid (TS) was 912.5 g/kg, and the volatile solid (VS),
crude protein, crude fat, nitrogen free extract content was
91.8%, 3.8%, 0.4%, and 5.2% based on TS.
For the inoculum, the digested residue from a biogas
reactor fed with pig manure was used as the original inoc-
ulum. The original inoculum was heated at 100 C for 15 min
and then cooled to room temperature in order to inhibit
hydrogen-consuming bacteria [11]. The heated inoculum with
pH 4.8, 1.52% TS, and 0.75% VS was used as the inoculum for
fermentative hydrogen production in this study.
The nutrition solution contained 80 g/L NH4HCO3, 12.4 g/L
KH2PO4,

Experimental design
Bottle test
The CS (3.2 g based on TS), inoculum (24 mL), the nutrient
solution (4 mL), and water (48.8 mL) were added to 150-mL
anaerobic bottles with initial substrate concentrations of
40 g TS/L. Initial pH of the mixed materials was adjusted to 7.0
with 1 M NaOH solution for all bottles. The bottles were purged
with N2 to create an anaerobic condition and sealed with a
butyl rubber stopper. The bottles were placed in a shaking
incubator at 35 C and 120 rpm for 72 h. The oxygen addition of
0, 0.70, 0.14, 0.21, 0.28, or 0.35 mL/(g TS$day) was carried out
using a syringe. Each oxygen addition test was run in three
parallel bottles.
Bench-scale test
The
scale-up
experiment
of
micro-aerobic
fermentative
hydrogen production was carried out in a bioreactor with a
total volume of 10 L (Fig. 1S). Based on the results of the bottle
test, the oxygen addition of 0.28 mL/(g TS$day) was selected
for the bench-scale test. The CS (320 g based on TS), the mixed
inoculum (2.4 L), the nutrient solution (0.4 L), and water (4.88 L)
were added to the fermenter. The initial pH of the mixed
materials was adjusted to 7.0 with the NaOH solution. The
fermenter was operated at 35 C for 72 h. As a comparison,
anaerobic fermentation was carried out in another bioreactor
without oxygen addition.
Analysis
TS and VS were determined according to standard methods
[12]. The pH and oxidation reduction potential (ORP) were
monitored using an online pH (HA405-DXK) and OPR meter
(PT4805-60) (Mettler Toledo, Switzerland) which was equipped
to bioreactor. Lignocellulose were determined using the Van
Soest method [13].
Biogas production was estimated by measuring the water
displacement in the case of the batch bottle test and by using
the LML-1 wet gas meter (Changchun Automobile Filter Co.,
Ltd, China) in the bench experiments. Biogas analysis was
performed using an Agilent 6890 gas chromatography (GC)
system (Agilent Technologies, USA) with a thermal conduc-
tivity detector (TCD) and a 2-m stainless steel column packed
with Porapak Q (50/80 mesh). The operating temperatures at
the injection port, column oven, and detector were 100, 70,
and 150 C, respectively. Argon at a ﬂow rate of 30 mL/min was
used as the carrier gas.
Liquid
samples
were
centrifuged
at
12,000
rpm
for
10 min at room temperature and ﬁltered with a 0.45-mm
membrane ﬁlter for analyzing the alkalinity, and volatile fatty
acid (VFA) concentrations. Alkalinity was determined using
the ZDJ-4B automatic potentiometric titrator (Shanghai Inesa
Instrument Co., Ltd., China) by the titration method [14].
Concentrations of the VFA (including acetate, propionate,
butyrate, iso-butyrate, valerate, and iso-valerate) in the su-
pernatant were measured after acidiﬁcation with 6 mol/L of
HCl using an Agilent 6820 GC (Agilent Technologies, USA)
equipped with a ﬂame ionization detector (FID) and a
30 m  0.25 mm  0.25 mm capillary column (DB-FFAP). The
temperatures at the injection port and detector were 250 and
300 C, respectively. The initial temperature of the column
oven was maintained at 50 C for 5 min, after which the
temperature was ramped at a rate of 10 C/min until a ﬁnal
temperature of 250 C was reached. The ﬁnal temperature was
maintained for 5 min. Nitrogen at a ﬂow rate of 1 mL/min was
used as the carrier gas [11]. Lactic acid was quantiﬁed using a
high-performance liquid chromatograph (Waters 2695, USA)
with a refractive index (RI) 2414 detector and a Shodex KC-
811 S-DVB gel Column. 0.1%H3PO4 was used as the mobile
phase at a ﬂow rate of 0.7 mL/min at 50 C [15].

DNA isolation and PCR-DGGE analysis
Total genomic DNA was extracted from sludge collected at
different fermentation time using a modiﬁed phenol/chloro-
form/isopropanol method [16]. For the PCR ampliﬁcation, the
universal primer setdincluding forward primer, 341F (50- CCT
ACGGGAGGCAGCAG -30), and reverse primer, 518R (50- ATTAC-
CGCGGCTGCTGG -30), and GC clamp (50- CGCCCGCCGCGCGC-
GGCGGGCGGGGCGGGGGCACGGGGGG -30)dwere used for the
PCR ampliﬁcation of the variable V3 region of 16S rDNA from
the puriﬁed genomic DNA. PCR ampliﬁcation was conducted
in an automated thermal cycler using the following protocol,
that is; initial denaturation for 4 min at 94 C, 30 cycles of
denaturation for 1 min at 94 C, annealing for 30 s at 55 C,
extension for 1 min at 72 C, followed by a ﬁnal extension for
10 min at 72 C.

analysis of PCR products was performed by electrophoresis for

gel containing a linear gradient of denaturant ranging from

Results and discussion
Determination of optimal oxygen addition
Hydrogen yields of bottle test with different amounts of added
oxygen are shown in Fig. 1. A maximum hydrogen yield of
27.5 mL/g VS was obtained for oxygen addition of 0.28 mL/(g
TS$day), which was 68.71% higher than that without oxygen
addition. These results indicated that the optimal oxygen
addition is 0.28 mL/(g TS$day) in micro-aerobic fermentative
hydrogen production.
Comparison on hydrogen production and lignocellulose
degradation
The modiﬁed Gompertz equation was used to appropriately
model the process of hydrogen production with a correlation
coefﬁcient (R2) of 0.9998 and 0.9986 for scale-up micro-aerobic
and anaerobic fermentative hydrogen production, respec-
tively. In addition to improving the hydrogen yield, the micro-
aerobic condition increased the hydrogen production rate and
increased hydrogen content in the later period (Fig. 2). The
positive effect of moderate oxygen addition is likely due to
improvement in the activity of facultative anaerobes or aer-
obes, which in turn increased the production of extracellular
hydrolytic enzymes. However, the cellular and enzymatic
mechanism of micro-aerobic fermentative hydrogen produc-
tion requires further study. It is worth mentioning that the
hydrogen yield of 41.6 mL/g VS from bench-scale test was
much greater than that of 27.5 mL/g VS from bottle test. This
may be due to the good mixing condition of scale-up biore-
actor. Therefore, there is space for micro-aerobic fermentative
hydrogen production through straw pretreatment, bioreactor
and process optimization.
The hemicellulose, cellulose, lignin, and ash contents of
raw CS and fermented residues are listed in Table 1. Hydrogen
production fermentation signiﬁcantly reduced the contents of
hemicellulose and cellulose, which are easily degradable. The
reduction of hemicellulose and cellulose was greater in micro-
aerobic fermentation than anaerobic fermentation, which
might be due to the enhanced hydrolysis resulting from the
oxygen addition.
Comparison on process parameters and by-products
The process parameters of ORP, pH, and alkalinity, and the by-
products of VFA were monitored during the process of
fermentative hydrogen production (Fig. 3). The ORP of micro-
aerobic fermentation (300 to 150 mV) was clearly higher
than that of anaerobic fermentation (560 to 360 mV), due to
the addition of oxygen. For micro-aerobic fermentation, it is
understandable that redox potential increased to higher value
through the fermentation, since oxygen was added everyday.

VFA accumulation decreases pH value. For anaerobic
fermentation, the pH value decreased from 7.0 to 4.9 with
accumulation of VFA, whereas it decreased to 4.7 in micro-
aerobic fermentation (Fig. 3a). While more VFA was pro-
duced with micro-aerobic fermentation, the pH of both fer-
mentations was similar during the period from 12 h to 36 h. In
general, the pH of the fermentation system was controlled by
a buffer system, and alkalinity was used to quantify the
buffering capacity. Fig. 3c shows the alkalinity obtained. An
obvious difference between the micro-aerobic and anaerobic
fermentation was observed for alkalinity during the period of
12e36 h, where 80% of the total hydrogen was produced. The
absolute reduction of alkalinity was 648 mg CaCO3/L for
micro-aerobic fermentation, and it was 1390 mg CaCO3/L for
anaerobic fermentation.
A modiﬁed buffer index (BI) is presented as Eq. (7) to eval-
uate the buffer ability of fermentative hydrogen production
system based on the traditional buffer index [19]. The lower BI
value indicates a strong buffer ability of fermentation system.
Here, the modiﬁed buffer index of micro-aerobic fermentation
and anaerobic fermentation were 668 and 1497. It seems that
the micro-aerobic condition had strong buffer ability to
tolerate higher VFA concentrations, which was helpful to
produce more hydrogen.

Comparison on bacterial community
An image of a DGGE gel of the PCR-ampliﬁed 16S rDNA seg-
ments extracted from the inoculum (Lane I), sludge sampled
from micro-aerobic fermentation (Lane M12 e M72) and
anaerobic fermentation (A12 e A72) at different fermentation
time is depicted in Fig. 4 (left). And corresponding band in-
tensity of DGGE is shown in Fig. 4 (right). The differences of
band numbers and band intensity were observed between
micro-aerobic and anaerobic fermentation. The number of
bands detected from the micro-aerobic condition was greater
than that from the anaerobic condition, suggesting microbial
community of micro-aerobic fermentation was more abun-
dant than that of anaerobic fermentation.
The Shannon-wiener index was used to evaluate the di-
versity of microbial community. The greater Shannon-wiener
index presents more abundant microbial community. The
Pielou index was used to evaluate the distribution evenness of
microbial community. The higher Pielou index indicates the
more even distribution of microbial species. The Shannon-
wiener and Pielou index were shown in Fig. 5. At the same
fermentation time, the diversity of microbial community
under micro-aerobic condition was richer than that under
anaerobic condition. On the contrary, distribution evenness of
microbial community under micro-aerobic condition was
poorer than that under anaerobic condition. This clearly in-
dicates that the dominant position of some bacteria in micro-
aerobic system is more obvious, even though the microbial
species of micro-aerobic system was more than that of
anaerobic system.

the bands were excised and puriﬁed to determine their 16S
rDNA sequences. A phylogenetic tree was then constructed by
comparing the obtained sequences with database sequences
using the BLAST search. The functions related to hydrogen

Bacteroides oleiciplenus (Band 4), Peptoclostridium difﬁcile (Band
6), Lactobacillus mucosae (Band 13 and 15), Clostridium butyricum
(Band 2),Clostridium baratii (Band 18), Biﬁdobacterium animalis
(Band 16 and 19), and an uncultured Clostridia bacterium (Band
17) existed in micro-aerobic and anaerobic fermentation sys-
tem. The Clostridia group is well-known to produce acetic acid,
n-butyric acid and hydrogen via dark fermentation based on
Eqs. (4) and (5) [20]. Citrobacter sp. (Band 5), Escherichia sp.
(Band12), and an uncultured Bacteroidetes bacterium (Band 9)
existed in the micro-aerobic system, but not in the anaerobic
system. Citrobacter sp. and Escherichia sp. were reported
facultative anaerobes producing hydrogen [21,22]. Promotion
of micro-aerobic condition is likely due to these bacteria.
Some bacteria were not detected in inoculum could come
from straw material.
Existence of B. animalis (Band 8, 16 and 19) and L. mucosae
(Band 13 and 15) might be responsible for the low hydrogen
production. These microorganisms can utilize carbohydrate-
rich substrate for the production of lactic acid, instead of
hydrogen [23], and other metabolites such as bacteriocins that
can inhibit the activity of hydrogen producing bacteria [24].
There are two categories of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) i.e.
homofermentative bacteria (Lactococcus and Lactobacillus) and
heterofermentative bacteria (Leuconostoc and Biﬁdobacterium).
Lactic acid is the only end product of glucose metabolism by
homofermentative bacteria through the Embden-Meyerhof-
Parnas (EMP) pathway as showed in the Eq. (8). Lactic, acetic
acid and CO2 are the end products of glucose metabolism by
heterofermentative bacteria through the biﬁdus pathway as
showed in the Eq. (9). The detected maximum lactic acid
concentrations were 1352 mg/L and 1400 mg/L for micro-
aerobic fermentation and anaerobic fermentation (Fig. 3b).

Therefore, B. animalis and L. mucosae that ferment monose
to lactate and acetate independent of hydrogen production
should be removed or inhibited in order to increase hydrogen
production. In especial, the removal or inactivation of indig-
enous microorganism L. mucosae existed in straw need to be
further studied.
Conclusion
The micro-aerobic condition was an effective method for
enhancing fermentative hydrogen production of straw. The
hydrogen yield of 41.6 mL/g VS obtained from bench-scale test
with oxygen addition of 0.28 mL/(g TS$day) was higher than
that of 28.9 mL/g VS without oxygen addition. The oxidation
reduction potential was 300 ~ 150 mV for micro-aerobic
fermentation.
Both
the
micro-aerobic
and
anaerobic
hydrogen productions were butyric acid-type fermentation.
Besides of Enterococcus, Bacteroides, Peptoclostridium, Clostridium
genera that existed both in micro-aerobic and anaerobic
fermentation system, Citrobacter sp. and Escherichia sp. were
unique to the micro-aerobic system. The presence of LAB
might lower fermentative hydrogen production.
